record_type_quote: The present study builds on the work of Yang et al. ( 2025 ), who explored undergraduate perspectives on AI ethics using ChatGPT as the focal technology. While their study offered valuable insights, it was conducted with a smaller sample (n = 110) in a single institutional setting, and it identified autonomy as the most valued ethic and justice as the least valued. In this replication and extension, we surveyed 200 undergraduates across diverse academic disciplines, aiming to confirm, refine, and expand upon the earlier findings.

targets.title: Undergraduate students’ perspectives of generative AI ethics.
targets.evidence_quote: The present study builds on the work of Yang et al. ( 2025 ), who explored undergraduate perspectives on AI ethics using ChatGPT as the focal technology. While their study offered valuable insights, it was conducted with a smaller sample (n = 110) in a single institutional setting, and it identified autonomy as the most valued ethic and justice as the least valued. In this replication and extension, we surveyed 200 undergraduates across diverse academic disciplines, aiming to confirm, refine, and expand upon the earlier findings.
targets.outcome_quote: In both this and earlier work, autonomy emerged as the most highly endorsed dimension, suggesting a shared concern among undergraduates that AI should enhance rather than diminish their capacity for independent learning and decision-making. However, differences emerge when considering the dimensions of justice and explicability . In the original study, disagreements in these areas were attributed largely to lack of awareness or limited exposure to AI’s technical workings.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The authors compare agreement on autonomy and explicit divergence on justice and explicability. The earlier finding identified justice as least valued, whereas this study places explicability lowest.
